Techradar has updated their Amazon Fire TV review

It's nice to see a site that keeps their reviews fresh. Techradar originally reviewed the Amazon Fire TV a year ago, but is keeping it relevant by adding periodic updates that may impact the score.

The rating is presently 4/5: "elegant and powerful but not as open as it would like you to think." Those words sum up my experience with the box exactly. I would prefer to be able to change the home screen, access Google Play Music, and get under the hood like with some of the more generic boxes, but the hardware is pretty impressive and relatively intuitive (the remote is quite nice, but the home screen is, in my opinion, a bit of a mess).

Blog: "Tunneling Data and Commands Over DNS to Bypass Firewalls"

OzymanDNS, TCP-over-DNS, Iodine, Dns2tcp, DNScat, DNSCat2, DeNiSe, and Heyuka are also used. Except for DNScat, which uses CNAMEs, these others use TXT or NULL recrods. And Heyuka does some EDNS0, but wrong. Immunity has a DNS tunnel but it's a joke. All are easy to spot and block. If DNS tunnels become popular, the ISPs and hotspot vendors will lock it all down: no third party iteration, and an RPZ of dns tunnel domains.

Evasion does not scale in DNS tunnels since hotspots and arubanets can blacklist faster than you can buy a new domain to host a new proxy. The one tool that survives will be SuDP, since it only uses slack space in DNS packets (only half used in 512 MTU, often). DPI costs too much for the hotspot market, compared to domain black lists. But SuDP is stopped by hotspots that prevent 3d party recursion. Many hotspots already do this, since it's one line in the firewall. That leaves only qname tunnels, and those must be under domains that can be blacklisted.

Popular DNS tunnels will ruin proxies for the rest of us. I think the blog post is interesting but a bad idea.
